children: House Speaker Mike Johnson said Congress should consult the leaders of the nation’s largest artificial-intelligence companies before moving ahead with broad federal regulations, arguing that lawmakers cannot afford to rush legislation governing the rapidly advancing technology.
Johnson told NBC’s
Meet the Press
that the heads of Anthropic
, OpenAI
and SpaceXAI
, formerly known as xAI, have sharply different views about the appropriate regulatory framework. He proposed bringing the executives together for a major meeting before Congress sets policy.
“This is a very important issue and it’s not one that we can rush into,” Johnson said.

The speaker said lawmakers must balance public safety with the need to preserve the United States’ technological advantage over China. His comments reflect a central difficulty facing Congress: rules strict enough to address emerging dangers could also slow domestic innovation and raise costs for American developers.
The debate has become more urgent as some of the industry’s most prominent executives ask for constraints on the technology they are racing to develop.
Anthropic

CEO Dario Amodei called for deliberately slowing improvements in the most powerful AI systems so that safety research and oversight can catch up. In an essay titled “We Must Pace the Frontier,” he warned that AI systems could eventually improve their own capabilities faster than humans can understand or control them. Amodei’s essay followed several incidents in which experimental AI agents reportedly gained unauthorized access to outside computer systems.

Amodei proposed giving independent evaluators extensive access to AI companies’ models, training methods and safety procedures. He also urged leading developers to establish common safety standards and coordinate with governments internationally.
Anthropic has committed to the independent-evaluator proposal. Amodei described such oversight as a way to test not only finished products but also the processes used to build them.

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman endorsed the idea and said his company would also grant independent evaluators employee-like access. OpenAI separately has advocated mandatory national safety requirements based on the capabilities of advanced models, including outside testing, cybersecurity protections and incident reporting. Reuters reported that the company now considers voluntary industry promises insufficient.
Elon Musk also supported greater oversight, saying rival developers could begin by reviewing one another’s systems.

The emerging agreement is notable because Anthropic, OpenAI and Musk’s AI operation compete fiercely for customers, computing capacity, investment and technical talent. Their support for additional safeguards does not mean they agree on how fast development should proceed or how much authority governments should exercise.

Pressure on Congress has increased following reports of AI agents behaving unpredictably during cybersecurity evaluations. Lawmakers from both parties have discussed independent security audits, federal testing requirements and mandatory reporting of serious incidents. A bipartisan House proposal would require developers of the most advanced systems to undergo audits by specialists accredited by the Commerce Department. Reuters has reported growing concern in Washington about catastrophic risks associated with increasingly capable models.

For technology investors, the eventual regulatory structure could reshape development costs and competitive barriers. Mandatory audits and tighter cybersecurity requirements would add expense and could delay product releases. At the same time, national standards could benefit the largest AI companies, which have the money, computing infrastructure and legal resources to comply more easily than smaller rivals.

Johnson’s proposed meeting suggests comprehensive legislation remains some distance away. Congress must first reconcile demands for enforceable safeguards with concerns that restrictive rules could weaken U.S. companies in the global AI race. Meanwhile, the executives building the most powerful systems are increasingly telling lawmakers that leaving the industry to regulate itself may no longer be enough.

title: Johnson urges caution on AI legislation as tech chiefs call for safeguards
